e-9512.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/4b5c788ad2c220b70a7f1d333680a70933f9b490a0db11fb3440dd3a2e06fa01.png)

Find a definite integral that's equivalent to the line integral $\displaystyle \int_C (x+y) \, \textrm{d} x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(3,3),$ as shown above.
e-9512.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}x  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(0,0)$ and $(3,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0+t(3-0),\,0+t(3-0)⟩ \\  & =⟨3t,\,3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x+y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3t+3t \\  & =6t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6t\cdot 3\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{1}t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9513.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to Y
e-9513.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/74033bfe17cefe62d5306b2186b9816ba26b816ece10c5dab5178abe1a9aaf89.png)

Find the definite integral equivalent to the line integral $\displaystyle\int_C x^2 \, \textrm d y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $25x^2 + 4y^2 = 100,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,5),$ as shown above.
e-9513.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 5\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}=4{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =20{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9521.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
e-9521.problem:
Evaluate $\displaystyle \int_C \left(x^2 + y^2\right)\,\textrm d y,$ where $C$ is the path along the upper-right quarter of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 4,$ traversed from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,2),$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/8fc3a36829c9780c34e13f253d607c3849bfd3ef1399a77a79a3dd3d30ef7140.png)
e-9521.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a quarter of a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-8\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,1)$ to the point $(2,2),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,t+1⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,1)$ and $(2,2).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(1+t(2-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,t+1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)+(t+1)^{2} \\  & =(3t-1)+({t}^{2}+2t+1) \\  & ={t}^{2}+5t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y2)dx, where C is the path along the line segment from the point (−1,1) to the point (2,2), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3t−1,t+1⟩.

a
∫01(t2+4t+2)dt
b
3∫01(t2+5t)dt
c
∫01(t2+5t)dt
d
3∫01(t2+5t+2)dt
e
3∫01(t2+4t+2)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (−1,1) and (2,2). It can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨(−1+t(2−(−1))),(1+t(2−1))⟩=⟨3t−1,t+1⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dxdt, we get the following: dxdt=ddt(3t−1)=3

Now, since f(x,y)=x+y2, we obtain f(r(t))=(3t−1)+(t+1)2=(3t−1)+(t2+2t+1)=t2+5t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫01f(r(t))dxdtdt=∫01(t2+5t)⋅3dt=3∫01(t2+5t)dt.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/43c8d1ced440e0fe79052c1329ff3af865e1fdbfb4cc0c7ad0a9c176592358e9.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,1)$ to the point $(2,2),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,t+1⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,1)$ and $(2,2).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(1+t(2-1))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,t+1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t-1)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)+(t+1)^{2} \\  & =(3t-1)+({t}^{2}+2t+1) \\  & ={t}^{2}+5t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+5t)\cdot 3\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+5t)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y)dx, where C is the path along a circle of radius 4, traversed from the point (−4,0) to the point (4,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
−4∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
b
−16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
c
−8∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
d
4∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
e
16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: The lower semicircle is traced by π≤t≤2π. Since x+y=4(cos t+sin t) and dx=-4 sin t dt, the integral becomes -16∫_π^{2π}(cos t+sin t)sin t dt, giving option b.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/9babf4c2ec631b3b872760261a46c3552cb93b93df90515ff0605c15043841ca.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y)dx, where C is the path along a circle of radius 4, traversed from the point (−4,0) to the point (4,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
−4∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
b
−16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
c
−8∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
d
4∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
e
16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 4 centered at O. It can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤2π.

Computing dxdt, we get the following: dxdt=ddt(4cos⁡t)=−4sin⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=x+y, we obtain f(r(t))=4cos⁡t+4sin⁡t=4(cos⁡t+sin⁡t).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫π2πf(r(t))dxdtdt=∫π2π4(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)⋅(−4sin⁡t)dt=−16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option b: for π≤t≤2π, x+y=4(cos t+sin t) and dx=-4 sin t dt. Multiplying gives -16(cos t+sin t)sin t dt. The displayed incorrect submission selected d, not b.

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dx, where C is the path along the ellipse 16x2+25y2=400, traversed from the point (0,−4) to the point (5,0), as shown above? Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨5cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
−10∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
b
−10∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
c
4∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
d
4∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
e
−5∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: The shown arc is traced for 3π/2≤t≤2π. Substituting x=5 cos t and y=4 sin t gives x−y=5 cos t−4 sin t and dx=−5 sin t dt. Thus the equivalent integral is option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/1b693165c8f6201e96f0a972746324c65a308d1f143f229c465b6aa22b7aeb16.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=400,$ traversed from the point $(0,-4)$ to the point $(5,0),$ as shown above?
*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-5{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dx, where C is the path along the ellipse 16x2+25y2=400, traversed from the point (0,−4) to the point (5,0), as shown above? Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨5cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
−10∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
b
−10∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
c
4∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
d
4∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
e
−5∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨5cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,3π2≤t≤2π.

Computing dxdt, we get the following: dxdt=ddt(5cos⁡t)=−5sin⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=x−y, we obtain f(r(t))=5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫3π/22πf(r(t))dxdtdt=∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)(−5sin⁡t)dt=−5∫3π/22π(5cos⁡t−4sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to X
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/1b693165c8f6201e96f0a972746324c65a308d1f143f229c465b6aa22b7aeb16.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=400,$ traversed from the point $(0,-4)$ to the point $(5,0),$ as shown above?
*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-5{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cyexdx, where C is the path along a circle of radius 2, traversed from the point (0,2) to the point (−2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩.

a
2∫π/2πe2sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
b
−4∫π/2πe2cos⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
−2∫π/2πe2cos⁡tsin⁡tdt
d
−4∫π/2πe2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
e
4∫π/2πe2sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: The arc corresponds to π/2≤t≤π. With x=2 cos t, y=2 sin t, and dx=−2 sin t dt, we get y e^x dx=−4e^(2 cos t)sin²t dt. Therefore option d is equivalent to the line integral.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/4727c988042bd8d63af370c507db8988b3024cf7e75c86d40bc70cdcfd744873.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}y{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cyexdx, where C is the path along a circle of radius 2, traversed from the point (0,2) to the point (−2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩.

a
2∫π/2πe2sin⁡tcos⁡tdt
b
−4∫π/2πe2cos⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
−2∫π/2πe2cos⁡tsin⁡tdt
d
−4∫π/2πe2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
e
4∫π/2πe2sin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 2 centered at O. It can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤π.

Computing dxdt, we get the following: dxdt=ddt(2cos⁡t)=−2sin⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=yex, we obtain f(r(t))=2sin⁡t⋅e2cos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫π/2πf(r(t))dxdtdt=∫π/2π2sin⁡t⋅e2cos⁡t⋅(−2sin⁡t)dt=−4∫π/2πe2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms d. For π/2≤t≤π, y e^x=2 sin t·e^(2 cos t) and dx=−2 sin t dt, giving −4∫ e^(2 cos t)sin²t dt with those bounds. The incorrect submission shown selected e.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to X
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/4727c988042bd8d63af370c507db8988b3024cf7e75c86d40bc70cdcfd744873.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}y{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $2,$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=y{e}^{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{e}^{2\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxy2dx, where C is the path along the ellipse 3x2+y2=3, traversed from the point (0,3) to the point (0,−3), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩.

a
−9∫π/23π/2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
b
−3∫π/23π/2cos3⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
−3∫π/23π/2cos⁡tsin3⁡tdt
d
9∫π/23π/2cos⁡tsin3⁡tdt
e
3∫π/23π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: The shown left half of the ellipse is traced for π/2≤t≤3π/2. Since xy²=3 cos t sin²t and dx=−sin t dt, direct substitution gives option c. Options b, d, and e also integrate to zero, but c directly expresses the parametrized line integral.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/2f01c4633489a913d93f86ccc83580963ea5cd41bed31347108730a7d60c3ebf.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3,$ traversed from the point $(0,\sqrt{3})$ to the point $(0,-\sqrt{3}),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxy2dx, where C is the path along the ellipse 3x2+y2=3, traversed from the point (0,3) to the point (0,−3), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩.

a
−9∫π/23π/2cos⁡tsin2⁡tdt
b
−3∫π/23π/2cos3⁡tsin⁡tdt
c
−3∫π/23π/2cos⁡tsin3⁡tdt
d
9∫π/23π/2cos⁡tsin3⁡tdt
e
3∫π/23π/2cos2⁡tsin⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫abf(r(t))dxdtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤3π2.

Computing dxdt, we get the following: dxdt=ddt(cos⁡t)=−sin⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=xy2, we obtain f(r(t))=cos⁡t⋅(3sin⁡t)2=3cos⁡tsin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫π/23π/2f(r(t))dxdtdt=∫π/23π/23cos⁡tsin2⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)dt=−3∫π/23π/2cos⁡tsin3⁡tdt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to X
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/2f01c4633489a913d93f86ccc83580963ea5cd41bed31347108730a7d60c3ebf.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=3,$ traversed from the point $(0,\sqrt{3})$ to the point $(0,-\sqrt{3}),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t{sin}^{3}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: For 0≤t≤1, x=3t−1, y=6t−2, and dy=6 dt. Thus xy=(3t−1)(6t−2)=2(9t²−6t+1), so the line integral equals 12∫₀¹(9t²−6t+1) dt, which is option b.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/36b985c811eb28d8220017c6b7407b3a104554d785dafdb35f17553c262bdc35.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}

Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along the line segment from the point (−1,−2) to the point (2,4), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3t−1,6t−2⟩.

a
18∫01(t2−6t+9)dt
b
12∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt
c
6∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt
d
12∫01(t2−6t+9)dt
e
18∫01(t2+6t+9)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (−1,−2) and (2,4). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(−1+t(2−(−1))),(−2+t(4−(−2)))⟩=⟨3t−1,6t−2⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dydt, we get the following:

dydt=ddt(6t−2)=6

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain

f(r(t))=(3t−1)⋅(6t−2)=18t2−12t+2.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫01f(r(t))dydtdt=∫01(18t2−12t+2)⋅6⋅dt=12∫01(9t2−6t+1)dt.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/36b985c811eb28d8220017c6b7407b3a104554d785dafdb35f17553c262bdc35.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-2)$ to the point $(2,4),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,4).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-2+t(4-(-2)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,6t-2⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t-2)=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)\cdot (6t-2) \\  & =18{t}^{2}-12t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18{t}^{2}-12t+2)\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-6t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along a quarter of the ellipse x2+4y2=4, traversed from the point (0,1) to the point (−2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩.

a
∫π/2π(2sin⁡t+cos⁡t)dt
b
2∫π/2π(sin⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt
c
2∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
d
2∫π/2πsin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
4∫π/2πsin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: The arc is traced for π/2≤t≤π. Since xy=2 cos t sin t and dy=cos t dt, the line integral becomes 2∫_{π/2}^{π}sin t cos²t dt, which is option c.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/4d02a56e1f927ccf8bd76a6fcc46dec61259649176695912865dd050657ce7f0.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydy, where C is the path along a quarter of the ellipse x2+4y2=4, traversed from the point (0,1) to the point (−2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩.

a
∫π/2π(2sin⁡t+cos⁡t)dt
b
2∫π/2π(sin⁡t+cos2⁡t)dt
c
2∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt
d
2∫π/2πsin⁡tcos⁡tdt
e
4∫π/2πsin2⁡tcos⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(sin⁡t)=cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain f(r(t))=2cos⁡tsin⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫π/2πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫π/2π2cos⁡tsin⁡t⋅cos⁡tdt=2∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c. For π/2≤t≤π, xy=2 cos t sin t and dy=cos t dt, so xy dy=2 sin t cos²t dt. The displayed incorrect submission selected a.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to Y
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/4d02a56e1f927ccf8bd76a6fcc46dec61259649176695912865dd050657ce7f0.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(-2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x2−y)dy, where C is the path along the line segment from the point (−1,−1) to the point (2,1), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3t−1,2t−1⟩.

a
6∫01(2t2+7t+1)dt
b
9∫01(2t2−t+7)dt
c
3∫01(6t2+5)dt
d
∫01(18t2+t)dt
e
2∫01(9t2−8t+2)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: For 0≤t≤1, x=3t−1, y=2t−1, and dy=2 dt. Hence x²−y=(3t−1)²−(2t−1)=9t²−8t+2. The equivalent integral is option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/58995f1bc5b45dbe0d30a9d0cbf704d792b955e7195c0e4dc3610ddf2e576579.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-1)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-1)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-1+t(1-(-1)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)^{2}-(2t-1) \\  & =9{t}^{2}-6t+1-2t+1 \\  & =9{t}^{2}-8t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x2−y)dy, where C is the path along the line segment from the point (−1,−1) to the point (2,1), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3t−1,2t−1⟩.

a
6∫01(2t2+7t+1)dt
b
9∫01(2t2−t+7)dt
c
3∫01(6t2+5)dt
d
∫01(18t2+t)dt
e
2∫01(9t2−8t+2)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (−1,−1) and (2,1). It can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨(−1+t(2−(−1))),(−1+t(1−(−1)))⟩=⟨3t−1,2t−1⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(2t−1)=2

Now, since f(x,y)=x2−y, we obtain f(r(t))=(3t−1)2−(2t−1)=9t2−6t+1−2t+1=9t2−8t+2.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫01f(r(t))dydtdt=∫01(9t2−8t+2)⋅2dt=2∫01(9t2−8t+2)dt.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/58995f1bc5b45dbe0d30a9d0cbf704d792b955e7195c0e4dc3610ddf2e576579.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment from the point $(-1,-1)$ to the point $(2,1),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(-1,-1)$ and $(2,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(-1+t(2-(-1))),\,(-1+t(1-(-1)))⟩ \\  & =⟨3t-1,\,2t-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t-1)^{2}-(2t-1) \\  & =9{t}^{2}-6t+1-2t+1 \\  & =9{t}^{2}-8t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}-8t+2)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(3x2+y2)dy, where C is the path along the ellipse 16x2+4y2=64, traversed from the point (−2,0) to the point (2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
8∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)sin⁡tdt
b
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt
c
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)sin2⁡tdt
d
4∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos2⁡tdt
e
16∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)cos⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: For π≤t≤2π, dy=4 cos t dt and 3x²+y²=12 cos²t+16 sin²t=4(3+sin²t). Multiplying gives option b. Option e also has integral zero, but b follows directly from the given parametrization.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/fd1956c8291f1bcecd7d37082110861ed7265fa40f7f85cbc69221cfdc5bea2d.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(3x2+y2)dy, where C is the path along the ellipse 16x2+4y2=64, traversed from the point (−2,0) to the point (2,0), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩.

a
8∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)sin⁡tdt
b
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt
c
16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)sin2⁡tdt
d
4∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos2⁡tdt
e
16∫π2π(3sin2⁡t+1)cos⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤2π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=3x2+y2, we obtain f(r(t))=3(2cos⁡t)2+(4sin⁡t)2=12cos2⁡t+16sin2⁡t=4sin2⁡t+12(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4sin2⁡t+12=4(sin2⁡t+3).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫π2πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫π2π4(sin2⁡t+3)⋅4cos⁡tdt=16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms b: on π≤t≤2π, 3x²+y²=4(sin²t+3) and dy=4 cos t dt. Their product gives the displayed integral in b. Option e also evaluates to zero, but b is the direct parametrized form.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to Y
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/fd1956c8291f1bcecd7d37082110861ed7265fa40f7f85cbc69221cfdc5bea2d.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(2,0),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =12{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡t+12 \\  & =4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }4({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡t+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

The curve C can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤2π.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(4sin⁡t)=4cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=3x2+y2, we obtain f(r(t))=3(2cos⁡t)2+(4sin⁡t)2=12cos2⁡t+16sin2⁡t=4sin2⁡t+12(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4sin2⁡t+12=4(sin2⁡t+3).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫π2πf(r(t))dydtdt=∫π2π4(sin2⁡t+3)⋅4cos⁡tdt=16∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos⁡tdt.

Your Answer:
4∫π2π(sin2⁡t+3)cos2⁡tdt

Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dy, where C is the path along a circle of radius 3, traversed from the point (0,−3) to the point (0,3), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩.

a
3∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos2⁡tdt
b
9∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
c
∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
d
3∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
e
9∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)sin2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: The right semicircle is traced for −π/2≤t≤π/2. Since x−y=3(cos t−sin t) and dy=3 cos t dt, the integral becomes 9∫_{−π/2}^{π/2}(cos t−sin t)cos t dt, which is option b.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/8d55ece1948f9ecb7da7d489b86a297651a34f409f83ba2470f6dd06678a375e.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $3,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dy, where C is the path along a circle of radius 3, traversed from the point (0,−3) to the point (0,3), as shown above?

Hint: Use the parametrization r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩.

a
3∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos2⁡tdt
b
9∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
c
∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt
d
3∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)sin⁡tdt
e
9∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 3 centered at O. It can be parameterized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,−π2≤t≤π2.

Computing dydt, we get the following: dydt=ddt(3sin⁡t)=3cos⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=x−y, we obtain f(r(t))=3cos⁡t−3sin⁡t=3(cos⁡t−sin⁡t).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫−π/2π/2f(r(t))dydtdt=∫−π/2π/23(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)⋅3cos⁡tdt=9∫−π/2π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos⁡tdt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals With Respect to Y
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/8d55ece1948f9ecb7da7d489b86a297651a34f409f83ba2470f6dd06678a375e.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along a circle of radius $3,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above?

*Hint: Use the parametrization $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.$*
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x-y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}3(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(2,2),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(2,0)$ and $(2,2).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(2+t(2-2)),\,(0+t(2-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})+{x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (2t)}{2})+(2)^{2} \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+4)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4+\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2(4t-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2[(4-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0)] \\  & =2[4-(-1)+1] \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

∫Cf(x,y)dy=∫abf(r(t))dydtdt.

The curve C is a line segment with endpoints (2,0) and (2,2). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨(2+t(2−2)),(0+t(2−0))⟩=⟨2,2t⟩, where 0≤t≤1.

Computing dydt, we get the following:

dydt=ddt(2t)=2

Now, since f(x,y)=πsin⁡(πy2)+x2, we obtain

f(r(t))=πsin⁡(π(2t)2)+(2)2=πsin⁡πt+4.

We can now evaluate the integral:

∫Cf(x,y)dx=∫01f(r(t))dydtdt=∫01(πsin⁡πt+4)⋅2⋅dt=2∫01(4+πsin⁡πt)dt=2(4t−cos⁡πt)|01=2[(4−cos⁡π)−(0−cos⁡0)]=2[4−(−1)+1]=12

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(2,0)$ and $(2,2).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(2+t(2-2)),\,(0+t(2-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi y}{2})+{x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi (2t)}{2})+(2)^{2} \\  & =\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+4.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t+4)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}(4+\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2(4t-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2[(4-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )-(0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0)] \\  & =2[4-(-1)+1] \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Parametrize the arc by x=4 cos t, y=sin t, with π≤t≤3π/2. On the ellipse, x²+16y²=16, and dx=−4 sin t dt, so the integrand times dx simplifies to −8 dt. The convergent improper integral at the starting endpoint is −8(3π/2−π)=−4π, giving b.

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}{8y}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the below-left quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(0,-1),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}{8y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+16(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{16({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-8{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8t\,{|}_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =-8(\frac{3\pi }{2}-\pi ) \\  & =-8(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a half of a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{1}{2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}[(1)^{3}-(-1)^{3}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}[(1)^{3}-(-1)^{3}] \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: On the ellipse, 1−y²=x²/9. Thus x e^(1−y²) dx=x e^(x²/9) dx=d[(9/2)e^(x²/9)]. Evaluating at the endpoints x=0 and x=3 gives (9/2)(e−1), which is option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14058598/assets/0e5257867dae67451500793687a2da24ee31a73a17c691d8d8a6dcded46e8993.png)

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x,$ where $C$ is the path along the three-quarters of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(3,0),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t){e}^{1-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t})\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={cos}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-9{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}[{e}^{1}-{e}^{0}] \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot (e-1) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(e-1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-9{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-9{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,(-\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}[{e}^{1}-{e}^{0}] \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot (e-1) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(e-1)\end{aligned}

decision.explanation: Use x=4 cos t and y=4 sin t for π≤t≤2π. Since x²+y²=16 and dy=4 cos t dt, the integrand times dy simplifies to 8 sin t dt. The singularity at x=0 cancels in the parametrized integrand, so the improper integral converges to [−8 cos t] from π to 2π, which is −16.

We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parameterized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y{x}^{2}+{y}^{3}}{8x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{3}}{8(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{64\operatorname{sin}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}{32\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }2\operatorname{tan}⁡t\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =-8[\operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ] \\  & =-8(1-(-1)) \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

$$
